title: Lincoln Financial's Third-Quarter Net Income Jumps to $1.4 Billion on Non-Operating Gains While Adjusted Operating Income Falls to $339 Million, and the Insurer Resumes Share Buybacks
summary: Lincoln National reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $1,399 million against $445 million a year earlier, but adjusted operating income available to common stockholders fell to $339 million from $397 million as Group Protection weakened, and the company resumed share repurchases with $50 million.
description:
Lincoln National Corporation, which operates as Lincoln Financial, published its results for the third quarter of 2026 in an earnings release furnished to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Form 8-K on November 5, 2026. The headline numbers point in two directions at once. Net income rose more than threefold, but the measure the company uses to describe its ongoing operations went down. This article sets out what the release reports, why the two measures differ and what the segment figures show. Every figure comes from the company's release unless this article says it was calculated here, and the release contains no forecast that this article repeats as a prediction.

Net income versus adjusted operating income

Net income was $1,399 million in the quarter, compared with $445 million a year earlier. After preferred dividends, net income available to common stockholders was $1,332 million against $411 million, which works out to $6.77 per diluted share against $2.12. For the first nine months of 2026, net income was $2,559 million against $423 million.

Adjusted operating income available to common stockholders, the measure that strips out items management considers outside day-to-day operations, moved the other way. It was $339 million, or $1.72 per diluted share, against $397 million, or $2.04, a year earlier. A direct comparison of the dollar amounts gives a decline of about 15%, and the per-share figure fell by about 16%, both calculated here. For nine months, adjusted operating earnings per share were $5.61 against $6.01, a decline of about 7% calculated here.

The release does not itemise every non-operating gain in the text this article draws on, so this article does not attribute the jump in net income to a specific cause beyond what the company states. What the release does state is that the annual assumption review, the yearly update of the actuarial assumptions behind its reserves, reduced GAAP earnings per share by $0.47 and adjusted earnings per share by $0.48 in the quarter.

Annuities

Annuities generated operating income of $294 million, down 5% from a year earlier, or $304 million excluding the annual assumption review. Sales were about $4.3 billion, down about 4% from the third quarter of 2025 but up 21% from the previous quarter. Net outflows were about $2.7 billion, which means that money leaving the business through withdrawals and surrenders exceeded money coming in, even with sales that large.

Life insurance

The Life segment earned $105 million, against $25 million a year earlier, or $130 million excluding the assumption review. Total life sales fell 64% to $106 million, while the company said core life sales rose 3%. The difference between the two figures indicates that the decline came from products outside the core line, though the release summary used here does not list which products those are.

Group Protection

Group Protection, which sells disability, life and dental coverage through employers, was the weak spot. Operating income was $46 million, against $149 million a year earlier. Excluding the assumption review it was $77 million, which the company put at a margin of 5.5%. Premiums rose 3% to $1.4 billion, but sales fell 38%. The release points to disability claim severity, meaning the cost of each claim, as a pressure on results. Chief executive Ellen Cooper acknowledged that Group Protection "fell short of our expectations."

Retirement Plan Services

Retirement Plan Services earned $55 million, up 20%. Net flows turned negative: the unit lost $1.9 billion on a net basis, against net inflows of $755 million a year earlier, and deposits fell 29% to $3.5 billion. Other Operations, which holds corporate items, reported a loss of $127 million against a loss of $99 million.

Capital and shareholder returns

Lincoln reported holding company liquidity of $1.0 billion, net of prefunding, which is about $350 million higher than at the end of 2025. It estimated its risk-based capital ratio, the regulatory measure of an insurer's capital relative to its risks, at above 420%. The company said it had "significantly improved financial flexibility" and, as a result, resumed share repurchases, starting with $50 million. It also retired $437 million of preferred stock through tender offers at a premium of $36 million, and declared preferred dividends of $34 million. The release summary reviewed for this article does not mention a common dividend, so this article makes no statement about one. A reinsurance transaction with Talcott closed in October 2026.

Book value per share was $46.17 including accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI), $84.05 excluding AOCI, and $80.63 on the company's adjusted basis. The gap between the first and second figures reflects unrealised losses on bonds: net unrealised losses on available-for-sale securities were $12.4 billion before tax, against $7.9 billion previously, which the company attributed to higher Treasury rates. These losses are on paper unless the securities are sold at a loss, but they reduce reported book value.

What to take from the quarter

The quarter shows a company that is repairing its capital position, evidenced by the preferred stock tender and the restart of buybacks, while its largest earnings engines are under pressure. Annuities and Group Protection earned less, and Retirement Plan Services had outflows. The release does not give a forecast, and this article does not offer one. Readers comparing life insurers should look at adjusted operating income, net flows, the assumption review impact and unrealised losses together, because any single figure, including the $1.4 billion net income, can mislead.
source_name: Lincoln National Corporation (third-quarter 2026 earnings release, Form 8-K filed with the SEC, November 5, 2026)
image_alt: Financial documents and calculator representing a life insurer's quarterly results (illustrative)
key_points: Net income was $1,399 million, or $6.77 per diluted share, against $445 million, or $2.12, in the third quarter of 2025, while adjusted operating income available to common stockholders fell to $339 million ($1.72 per share) from $397 million ($2.04).
Group Protection operating income dropped to $46 million from $149 million, or $77 million excluding the annual assumption review, and the company said the result fell short of its expectations.

Annuities earned $294 million, down 5%, on sales of about $4.3 billion; Life earned $105 million against $25 million; Retirement Plan Services earned $55 million, up 20%, but had net outflows of $1.9 billion.
Lincoln resumed share repurchases with $50 million, retired $437 million of preferred stock through tender offers, and reported holding company liquidity of $1.0 billion net of prefunding.

The annual assumption review reduced GAAP earnings per share by $0.47 and adjusted earnings per share by $0.48, and net unrealized losses on available-for-sale securities rose to $12.4 billion before tax.
why_it_matters: Lincoln is one of the largest US providers of annuities, life insurance and workplace benefits, so its results show how a life insurer can report a very large headline profit while its recurring operating earnings shrink. Investors, policyholders and employers who buy its group products should read the operating figures, the segment detail and the balance-sheet items together, not the net income number alone.

title: Brighthouse Financial's Third-Quarter Adjusted Earnings Fall to $527 Million as the Company Awaits State Approval of Its $4.1 Billion Sale to an Aquarian Capital Affiliate
summary: Brighthouse Financial reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $302 million and adjusted earnings of $527 million, down from $453 million and $970 million, while disclosing that Delaware, New York and Massachusetts approvals for its $70-per-share sale to an Aquarian Capital affiliate are not expected before the December 6, 2026 outside date.
description:
Brighthouse Financial, Inc. published its third-quarter 2026 results in an earnings press release furnished to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Form 8-K on November 5, 2026. The release is notable for two reasons. The earnings figures are sharply lower than a year earlier, and the company states that regulatory approvals for its pending sale will not arrive by the contractual outside date. This article reports both, using the company's own figures. Where a number was calculated here rather than reported, the text says so.

Earnings

Net income available to shareholders was $302 million, or $5.21 per share, against $453 million, or $7.89, in the third quarter of 2025. Adjusted earnings, the company's measure that excludes certain market-related and other items, were $527 million, or $9.12 per share, against $970 million, or $16.87.

The comparison is distorted by the annual actuarial assumption review. The release reports notable items, which it ties to that review, of $314 million favourable ($5.42 per share) this quarter and $709 million favourable ($12.33 per share) a year earlier. Removing them gives adjusted earnings of $213 million ($3.68) against $261 million ($4.54). On that basis, earnings fell by about 18% in dollar terms, calculated here, a much smaller decline than the 46% drop in the headline adjusted figure, also calculated here. Readers should therefore treat the headline adjusted number as heavily influenced by the review. Corporate expenses were $204 million.

Segments

Adjusted earnings by segment were $301 million for Annuities, $91 million for Life, $166 million for Run-off and a loss of $31 million for Corporate and Other, which sum to the $527 million total. Run-off holds products the company no longer actively sells.

Sales

Annuity sales were $2.4 billion, unchanged from the second quarter, down 12% from the third quarter of 2025 and down 8% for the year to date. Shield Level Annuities, which offer a degree of protection against market losses in exchange for capped upside, made up $2.1 billion of the total. Life insurance sales were $36 million.

Balance sheet and capital

Book value was $3.3 billion, or $57.59 per share. Excluding accumulated other comprehensive income, which captures unrealised gains and losses on investments, book value was $9.3 billion, or $161.36 per share. The large difference between the two shows how much unrealised investment losses weigh on reported book value.

The company estimated its combined risk-based capital ratio at 415 to 435 percent, within its 400 to 450 percent target range. Preliminary statutory combined total adjusted capital was $4.8 billion. Holding company liquid assets were $1.0 billion. The release says the capital ratio benefited from a $600 million extraordinary dividend from Brighthouse Reinsurance Company of Delaware, a subsidiary. Net investment income was $1,257 million, adjusted net investment income was $1,310 million, and the adjusted yield was 4.41%. Policyholder account balances were $88.8 billion and separate account assets were $81.6 billion.

The pending acquisition

The release confirms that an affiliate of Aquarian Capital has agreed to acquire Brighthouse for $70.00 per share in cash, a value of about $4.1 billion. Completion needs approval from the insurance regulators in Delaware, New York and Massachusetts, and those approvals are still outstanding. The agreement's outside date, after which either side could in principle walk away, has been automatically extended to December 6, 2026. The release states that the approvals are not expected by that date and that the parties are discussing an extension, with no assurance that one will be agreed.

That wording matters. It means the deal has no confirmed closing date, and the company is telling investors in plain terms that the timetable has slipped. The release does not say why the approvals are taking longer, and this article does not speculate. The release summary reviewed for this article does not mention a share buyback and contains no executive quotes, so this article makes no statement about either.

How to read the comparison

Two cautions apply when comparing this quarter with last year. First, the notable items are large relative to the underlying figures in both periods, so a change in the size of the favourable actuarial review can move headline adjusted earnings by hundreds of millions of dollars without any change in the business. Second, the per-share figures depend on the share count, which the release summary does not detail here, so the dollar comparisons above are the more reliable guide.

What it means for policyholders

Brighthouse's contracts are obligations of its insurance subsidiaries, which remain subject to state regulation and the capital requirements described above. The release does not describe any change to existing contracts as a result of the proposed sale, and this article does not suggest one. Policyholders who want to understand their position should read the statutory filings of their specific issuing company and contact their state insurance department with questions.

Summary

The quarter shows lower underlying earnings once the actuarial review is stripped out, steady but declining annuity sales, and a capital ratio inside the company's target range that was supported by a one-off subsidiary dividend. The more consequential item may be the regulatory timetable. If the parties cannot agree an extension by December 6, the release says there is no assurance either way, and anyone with money at stake in the deal should watch for the company's next filing.
source_name: Brighthouse Financial, Inc. (third-quarter 2026 earnings press release, Form 8-K filed with the SEC, November 5, 2026)
image_alt: Financial documents and a laptop representing an annuity insurer's quarterly results (illustrative)
key_points: Net income available to shareholders was $302 million ($5.21 per share) against $453 million ($7.89), and adjusted earnings were $527 million ($9.12) against $970 million ($16.87).

Both years include large favourable notable items tied to the annual actuarial review: $314 million this quarter and $709 million a year earlier, so adjusted earnings excluding notable items were $213 million ($3.68) against $261 million ($4.54).
Annuity sales were $2.4 billion, flat from the previous quarter and down 12% from a year earlier, with Shield Level Annuities accounting for $2.1 billion; life sales were $36 million.

An affiliate of Aquarian Capital has agreed to acquire the company for $70.00 per share in cash, about $4.1 billion, but approvals from three state insurance regulators are outstanding and the release says they are not expected by the December 6, 2026 outside date.

Combined risk-based capital was estimated at 415 to 435 percent against a 400 to 450 percent target range, helped by a $600 million extraordinary dividend from Brighthouse Reinsurance Company of Delaware.
why_it_matters: Brighthouse sells annuities and life insurance to retail customers, and its sale to a private-capital-backed buyer is the kind of deal that state insurance regulators scrutinise closely. The company's own statement that approvals will not arrive by the outside date shows how long such reviews can take and what shareholders and policyholders are waiting on.

title: Equitable Holdings' Third-Quarter Operating Earnings Climb to $595 Million and Assets Reach $1.16 Trillion as Its Planned Merger With Corebridge Heads Toward a Year-End Close
summary: Equitable Holdings reported third-quarter 2026 non-GAAP operating earnings of $595 million, or $2.13 per share, up from $455 million and $1.48, with net income of $1,121 million, assets under management and administration of $1,156 billion and $320 million returned to shareholders, while its merger with Corebridge is expected to close by year-end 2026.
description:
Equitable Holdings, Inc. released its third-quarter 2026 results in an earnings release furnished to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Form 8-K, with the release dated November 2, 2026. The company reported sharply higher earnings on both a GAAP and a non-GAAP basis, a larger asset base and continued capital returns. It also confirmed that its merger with Corebridge is expected to close by the end of 2026. This article reports the figures from the release and points out one discrepancy between the release's own percentage descriptions and a direct calculation of its numbers.

Net income and operating earnings

Net income attributable to Holdings was $1,121 million, or $4.05 per diluted share. In the third quarter of 2025 the company reported a net loss of $1,309 million, or $4.47 per share. The release does not break down the GAAP swing in the text used here, so this article does not assign it to a cause.

Non-GAAP operating earnings were $595 million, or $2.13 per share, against $455 million, or $1.48. The release also gives a figure excluding notable items, which are specific items management separates out: $554 million, or $1.98 per share, against $510 million. For the nine months to September 30, operating earnings per share were $5.43 against $3.90.

A discrepancy worth flagging

The release describes operating earnings per share growth with percentages that do not match a direct calculation of its own numbers. Going from $1.48 to $2.13 is an increase of about 44%, calculated here, yet the release describes the quarter as "up 19%." For the nine months, $3.90 to $5.43 is about 39%, calculated here, while the release says "up 22%." The release does not explain the difference in the portion reviewed. This article does not offer an explanation for the gap. Readers should rely on the dollar and per-share figures, which are internally consistent, and treat the percentage descriptions with caution.

Segments

Segment operating earnings, using the release's segment names, were $432 million for Retirement against $405 million, $152 million for Asset Management against $154 million, $75 million for Wealth Management against $59 million, and a loss of $64 million for Corporate and Other against a loss of $163 million. They add to the $595 million total, and last year's figures add to $455 million. That arithmetic shows where the improvement came from: the narrower corporate loss contributed $99 million of the $140 million increase, calculated here, while Retirement added $27 million and Wealth Management added $16 million.

Retirement

Retirement's total assets were $189.0 billion against $171.7 billion. The segment recorded net inflows of $1.1 billion and first-year premiums of $6.2 billion, up 14%.

Asset management

AllianceBernstein, the listed asset manager in which Equitable holds an interest, ended the quarter with assets under management of $900.4 billion against $860.1 billion a year earlier. Net inflows were $6.6 billion, against net outflows of $2.3 billion in the third quarter of 2025. The swing from outflows to inflows is one of the clearest operating improvements in the release, although segment operating earnings for Asset Management were essentially flat.

Wealth Management

Wealth Management assets under administration were $140.4 billion against $118.2 billion, and advisory net new assets were $2.7 billion against $2.2 billion.

Group assets

Total assets under management and administration were $1,156 billion, up from $1,110 billion a year earlier, an increase of about 4% calculated here.

Capital returns

Equitable returned $320 million to shareholders in the quarter: $82 million in dividends and $238 million in share repurchases. That represents a payout ratio of 59%. The company said it is on track for a payout of 60% to 70% for 2026.

The Corebridge merger

Investors tracking the transaction should note the wording. The release states that the merger with Corebridge is expected to close by year-end 2026, subject to regulatory approvals. The portion of the release reviewed does not provide the deal terms, the exchange ratio or the list of approvals still needed, and this article does not supply them. Because closing depends on regulators, the year-end expectation is a company estimate, not a certainty.

Management commentary

Segment earnings in Asset Management dipped by $2 million, from $154 million to $152 million, calculated here, so the segment's operating profit was essentially unchanged despite the flow improvement.

Chief executive Mark Pearson said the company continues to see "tremendous demand for the financial advice and retirement, protection, and asset management solutions we provide."

Summary

In short, the quarter shows higher operating earnings across the board except Asset Management, a much narrower corporate loss, growing assets and healthy flows at AllianceBernstein. The main caution is the mismatch between the release's percentage descriptions and its own figures. As always with insurer results, the non-GAAP measures are management's choice of what to include, and readers should compare them with the GAAP net income that the company also reports.
source_name: Equitable Holdings, Inc. (third-quarter 2026 earnings release, Form 8-K filed with the SEC, November 2, 2026)
image_alt: Charts and figures on a desk representing an insurer and asset manager's quarterly results (illustrative)
key_points: Non-GAAP operating earnings were $595 million, or $2.13 per share, against $455 million, or $1.48; excluding notable items they were $554 million ($1.98) against $510 million.
Net income attributable to Holdings was $1,121 million, or $4.05 per diluted share, against a loss of $1,309 million, or $4.47 per share, a year earlier.
Retirement earned $432 million, Asset Management $152 million and Wealth Management $75 million, while the Corporate and Other loss narrowed to $64 million from $163 million.
Total assets under management and administration were $1,156 billion against $1,110 billion, with AllianceBernstein assets at $900.4 billion and net inflows of $6.6 billion.
The company returned $320 million to shareholders, a 59% payout, and said its planned merger with Corebridge is expected to close by year-end 2026, subject to regulatory approvals.
why_it_matters: Equitable combines a retirement and annuity business, a wealth-management arm and the asset manager AllianceBernstein, so its results show how a diversified US financial group earns money from retirement savers. Because it plans to merge with Corebridge, its quarter is also a baseline for anyone judging what the combined company will look like.

title: Principal Financial Group's Third-Quarter Operating Earnings Per Share Rise 6% to $2.22 as Life Insurance Swings to a Profit, International Pensions Slide 38% and Assets Under Management Hold at $785 Billion
summary: Principal Financial Group reported third-quarter 2026 non-GAAP operating earnings of $481.8 million, or $2.22 per share, up 6% per share, with net income of $631.9 million, assets under management flat at $785.0 billion and $429 million returned to shareholders, and it set a fourth-quarter dividend of $0.85 per share.
description:
Principal Financial Group, Inc. has published its third-quarter 2026 results in an earnings release filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission as an exhibit to a current report. The exhibit as retrieved for this article does not display an issue date, but the company's earnings call took place on Tuesday, October 27, 2026. The results show modest growth in operating earnings per share, a recovery in life insurance, weaker international pensions and negative net cash flow in asset management. This article reports the figures as published, and flags where it has calculated a number itself.

Net income and operating earnings

Net income attributable to Principal Financial Group was $631.9 million, or $2.91 per share, against $213.8 million, or $0.95, in the third quarter of 2025. The company also reports non-GAAP net income excluding an exited business: $354.8 million, or $1.64 per share, against $465.6 million, or $2.06. The two comparisons point in opposite directions, which shows how much the exited business affects the GAAP figure. The release as reviewed does not explain which items drove the GAAP result, and this article does not guess.

The company's main measure is non-GAAP operating earnings. It was $481.8 million, or $2.22 per share, against $2.10 a year earlier, an increase of 6% per share. Excluding significant variances, which are items management considers unusual, operating earnings were $540.6 million, or $2.49 per share, against $2.32, an increase of 7%.

Segment results

The release reports pre-tax operating earnings by segment. Total pre-tax operating earnings were $587.5 million against $579.9 million.

Retirement and Income Solutions earned $297.8 million against $310.3 million, a 4% decline, while its net revenue rose 1% to $757.3 million.

Principal Asset Management earned $230.5 million against $274.7 million. It has two parts. Investment Management earned $168.1 million against $173.5 million, with assets under management of $581.7 billion, down 3%. International Pension earned $62.4 million against $101.2 million, a 38% fall, even though its assets under management rose 10% to $166.2 billion. The release summary used here does not explain why earnings fell as assets grew, so this article does not offer a reason.

Benefits and Protection earned $169.7 million against $86.5 million, nearly double. Within it, Specialty Benefits earned $137.3 million against $155.5 million, a 12% fall, although premium and fees rose 6%. Life insurance earned $32.4 million against a loss of $69.0 million, a swing of $101.4 million calculated here, which accounts for more than the entire segment improvement of $83.2 million, also calculated here. The Corporate segment lost $110.5 million against a loss of $91.6 million.

Assets and flows

Assets under management were $785.0 billion, essentially flat against $784.3 billion. Assets under administration, which include assets the company administers but does not manage, were $1,840.3 billion, up 3%. Net cash flow for assets under management was an outflow of $10.7 billion, against an inflow of $0.4 billion a year earlier. Flat assets alongside a $10.7 billion outflow indicates that market movements or other factors offset the withdrawals, though the portion of the release reviewed does not give the split.

Capital and dividend

Principal returned $429 million to shareholders in the quarter, made up of $250 million in share repurchases and $179 million in dividends. It reported excess and available capital of $1.5 billion. The board set a fourth-quarter common dividend of $0.85 per share, which is $0.01 higher than the previous quarter and 8% higher than a year earlier. It is payable on December 18 to shareholders of record on December 2. Annualised, $0.85 per quarter would be $3.40 per share, calculated here, although the board declares each dividend separately and the release gives no commitment beyond this one. Of the $429 million returned in the quarter, buybacks were about 58% and dividends about 42%, calculated here.

Management commentary

Chief executive Deanna Strable said: "We grew earnings per share, continued to build momentum in the markets where we're focused."

Reading the results

Three points stand out. First, total pre-tax segment earnings rose only about 1%, calculated here ($587.5 million against $579.9 million), so the underlying segment picture is steadier than the 6% per-share headline might suggest. Second, the improvement in life insurance offset lower earnings in Specialty Benefits, International Pension and Retirement and Income Solutions, which means the mix of earnings changed more than the total. Third, the $10.7 billion outflow in assets under management is a reminder that flat balances can hide changing flows. The release as reviewed does not give the prior-year operating earnings in dollars or the share count, so this article does not attempt to explain the gap between earnings growth and per-share growth.

What the release does not tell us

The portion reviewed does not provide guidance for future quarters, and this article does not offer a forecast. It also does not separate the contribution of market performance from client flows. Anyone relying on these figures for a decision should read the full exhibit, which includes reconciliations of the non-GAAP measures to the GAAP results.
source_name: Principal Financial Group, Inc. (third-quarter 2026 earnings release, SEC Exhibit 99; earnings call held October 27, 2026)
image_alt: Charts and reports representing a retirement and asset management group's quarterly results (illustrative)
key_points: Non-GAAP operating earnings were $481.8 million, or $2.22 per share, up 6% per share from $2.10; excluding significant variances they were $540.6 million, or $2.49, up 7% from $2.32.

Net income attributable to the company was $631.9 million, or $2.91 per share, against $213.8 million, or $0.95; excluding the exited business, non-GAAP net income was $354.8 million ($1.64) against $465.6 million ($2.06).

Pre-tax operating earnings by segment: Retirement and Income Solutions $297.8 million (down 4%), Principal Asset Management $230.5 million against $274.7 million, and Benefits and Protection $169.7 million against $86.5 million.

Assets under management were $785.0 billion against $784.3 billion, and assets under administration were $1,840.3 billion, up 3%, but AUM net cash flow was negative $10.7 billion against $0.4 billion.

The company returned $429 million to shareholders ($250 million in buybacks and $179 million in dividends) and set a fourth-quarter dividend of $0.85 per share, payable December 18 to holders of record on December 2.
why_it_matters: Principal manages retirement plans, asset management and workplace benefits for businesses and individuals, so its quarter shows how pension savings, investment flows and employee-benefit claims are affecting a large US financial group. The mix of rising per-share earnings, a swing in life insurance and net outflows from investment products is a useful reference for employers and savers.

title: ASIC's 2026-27 General Insurance Priorities: A Review of 'Disaster Chasers' and Claims Management Firms, Motor Premium Disclosure Failures and Cash Settlements After Cyclone Jasper
summary: In a letter dated 30 September 2026, ASIC set its general insurance priorities for 2026-27, announcing a review of for-profit claims management firms and 'disaster chasers', and reporting on motor premium disclosure and cash settlements of at least 63% of finalised Cyclone Jasper home claims.
description:
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) has told general insurers where it will concentrate its supervision in 2026-27. The priorities appear in a supervisory letter dated 30 September 2026, signed by ASIC Commissioner Alan Kirkland. The letter combines one new activity, a review of for-profit claims management firms, with follow-up on earlier work on motor insurance premiums and on cash settlements after Cyclone Jasper. It also sets out how ASIC will coordinate with other regulators. This article summarises the letter and states plainly what it does not cover.

A new review of claims management firms

The main new item is a review of for-profit claims management firms, including those described as disaster chasers. These businesses help consumers with home insurance claims, often after a major weather event. ASIC says the review started in the first quarter of 2026-27.

The letter lists the concerns. ASIC wants to examine how these firms sell their services and acquire clients, the fee and cancellation terms they impose, the role they play in claims handling and complaints handling, and their relationships with repairers and suppliers. ASIC says it will seek information from insurers and from the firms themselves "to identify any practices that may result in consumer harm."

The wording is careful. The letter identifies concerns to be examined, not findings of misconduct, and this article does not suggest that any named firm has breached the law. For consumers, the practical point is that anyone who hires a third party to manage a home claim should read the fee and cancellation terms first.

Motor insurance premium disclosure

The letter reports on ASIC's review of how insurers disclose motor premiums, published as Report 838 (REP 838). ASIC found that no sampled insurer explained the key factors behind a premium or why it had changed. Insurers that charged more for paying by instalments did not clearly state that paying annually could save 10 to 20 percent. Five insurers did not compare year-on-year changes in key policy features, such as the excess and the insured value, in their renewal notices.

ASIC wants clearer quote and renewal documents, and says it has given individual feedback to the insurers it sampled. The letter does not announce enforcement action in connection with the review.

Cash settlements after Cyclone Jasper

The third item concerns home claims after Cyclone Jasper. ASIC found that at least 63% of finalised home claims included a cash settlement. Offers were often based on quotes from the insurer's preferred suppliers, and ASIC has doubts about whether those offers cover what repairs actually cost. It also found that insurers need to give clearer information about what a settlement includes and what review rights the policyholder has, that vulnerable consumers were not always identified, and that insurers lacked data on how their offers changed during negotiation.

ASIC has asked all insurers to act on these points and says it will monitor progress through its supervision. The letter does not state what an adequate settlement should be, and it does not set a deadline for the changes.

Industry code and wider reviews

The letter notes that the Insurance Council of Australia plans to seek ASIC approval of a new General Insurance Code, after public consultation in July 2026. ASIC says it will assess the code under Regulatory Guide 183. Insurers may also be drawn into wider ASIC reviews of sustainability reporting, governance and financial reporting.

Working with other bodies

ASIC says it will work with the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA), the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) and the General Insurance Code Governance Committee. It will engage with members of the Council of Financial Regulators on cyber risks, and will harmonise data collection under the Council's Better Regulation roadmap. ASIC also invites examples of unnecessary regulatory burden from the industry.

What the letter does not say

The letter sets no compliance deadlines other than the first-quarter 2026-27 start of the claims management review. It does not address add-on insurance products or premium funding, so readers should not assume those are covered. It is also a supervisory letter, not legislation or a legally binding rule, so its practical effect depends on how ASIC follows up with individual insurers.

What policyholders can do

These suggestions are drawn from the issues ASIC raised, not from advice in the letter itself.

The letter points to several practical steps. When a quote or renewal arrives, compare the excess and insured value with last year's, because ASIC found some insurers did not make that easy. If paying by instalments, ask what the annual price would be. If offered a cash settlement after a disaster, ask what it includes, how it was calculated and what the review rights are. Consumers who are unhappy with an outcome can raise a complaint with their insurer and, if it is not resolved, with AFCA.
source_name: Australian Securities and Investments Commission (supervisory letter to general insurers, 30 September 2026)
image_alt: Generic photograph illustrating a story about insurance regulation (illustrative)
key_points: The letter, dated 30 September 2026 and signed by ASIC Commissioner Alan Kirkland, announces a new review of for-profit claims management firms, including so-called disaster chasers who help consumers with home claims, starting in the first quarter of 2026-27.

ASIC will ask insurers and these firms for information to identify practices that may cause consumer harm, covering sales and client acquisition, fee and cancellation terms, roles in claims and complaints handling, and relationships with repairers and suppliers.

In its motor premium review (REP 838), ASIC found that no sampled insurer explained the key factors behind premiums or why they changed, and that insurers charging more for instalments did not clearly say paying annually could save 10 to 20 percent.

After Cyclone Jasper, at least 63% of finalised home claims included a cash settlement, and ASIC found offers were often based on preferred-supplier quotes, raising doubts about whether they cover repair costs.
The Insurance Council of Australia plans to seek ASIC approval of a new General Insurance Code, which ASIC will assess under RG 183.
why_it_matters: Australian households rely on general insurers for home, motor and contents cover, and claims after severe weather are when that cover is tested. ASIC's letter tells insurers what the regulator will examine in the coming year and gives consumers a view of the practices it considers risky, including paying a third party to run a home claim.

title: India's Insurance and Lending Platforms Report Strong Quarters: PB Fintech's Profit Rises 43% to Rs 192 Crore, Bajaj Finserv Earns Rs 5,952 Crore and Max Financial's Half-Year Profit More Than Doubles
summary: Three listed Indian financial groups reported results in late October and early November 2026: PB Fintech's profit rose 43% to Rs 192 crore, Bajaj Finserv's consolidated profit rose 25% to Rs 5,952 crore, and Max Financial's half-year profit reached Rs 219 crore, according to secondary summaries of their stock-exchange filings.
description:
Three of India's best-known listed financial groups have reported results for the quarter or half-year ended September 30, 2026: PB Fintech, Max Financial Services and Bajaj Finserv. The figures below come from secondary summaries of the companies' results that were published on the investor-news site Investywise, dated October 30, October 27 and in the case of Bajaj Finserv following board approval on November 3, 2026. The stock-exchange filings themselves were not reviewed for this article, so the numbers should be checked against the filings on the BSE or NSE before anyone relies on them. In India, a crore is ten million rupees.

PB Fintech

PB Fintech operates Policybazaar, an online insurance marketplace, and Paisabazaar, a lending marketplace. For the second quarter of fiscal 2027 (July to September 2026), the summary reports profit after tax of Rs 192 crore, up 43% from a year earlier, and a profit margin that rose from 8% to 9%. Operating revenue was Rs 2,178 crore, up 35%.

Total insurance premium sold through the platform was Rs 9,385 crore, up 38%. New protection premium, which covers health and term life insurance, rose 42%. Core online insurance premium rose 38%. Lending disbursals rose 22%, which the summary describes as the fifth consecutive quarter of sequential growth.

For the first half, total revenue was Rs 4,066 crore, up 37%, and profit after tax was Rs 355 crore, up 62%. New protection premium rose 47%, core online premium rose 39% and lending disbursals rose 27%. The summary also says revenue has grown at a compound annual rate of 51% between the second quarter of FY22 and the second quarter of FY27, and that the profit margin has moved from negative 73% to 9% over the same period. The summary does not give an EBITDA figure or a split of profit between Policybazaar and Paisabazaar.

Max Financial Services

Max Financial Services is the holding company for Axis Max Life Insurance. The summary reports consolidated profit after tax of Rs 219 crore for the first half of FY27, up 137%. The prior-year base is not given, so this article cannot restate the earlier figure. Revenue excluding investment income was Rs 17,484 crore, up 16%.

At Axis Max Life, annualised premium equivalent (APE), a measure that standardises single and regular premiums, was Rs 4,638 crore, up 11%. Value of new business (VNB), the present value of profits expected from policies sold in the period, was Rs 1,180 crore, up 21%. Profit before tax was Rs 234 crore, up 35%. The solvency ratio was 197%, and the claims paid ratio for FY26 was 99.8%. The summary covers the half-year only and does not give a VNB margin, an embedded value or assets under management.

Bajaj Finserv

For the second quarter of FY27, Bajaj Finserv reported consolidated total income of Rs 43,416 crore, up 17% from Rs 37,215 crore, and consolidated profit after tax of Rs 5,952 crore, up 25% from Rs 4,746 crore. Profit attributable to owners of the company was Rs 2,758 crore, up 23%. Both percentages match a direct calculation of the stated figures, about 17% and 25%, calculated here.

Standalone income was Rs 2,047.15 crore and standalone profit after tax was Rs 1,458.53 crore. Among its subsidiaries, Bajaj Finance reported profit after tax of Rs 6,367 crore, up 29%. Bajaj General Insurance reported profit after tax of Rs 420 crore, and Bajaj Life Insurance reported value of new business of Rs 512 crore, up 40%. The summary uses the names Bajaj General Insurance and Bajaj Life Insurance, and this article follows it. It does not give gross written premium or a combined ratio for the general insurer, so those cannot be assessed here.

What the three have in common

All three groups report growth in the insurance-related measures that matter most for each business model. For PB Fintech, it is premium sold and new protection premium. For Max Financial, it is APE and VNB. For Bajaj Finserv, it is VNB and group profit. In each case, profit grew faster than revenue or premium, which indicates improving profitability, although the summaries do not explain the reasons and this article does not offer any.

Limits of this comparison

The three companies report on different bases and for different periods: one quarter for PB Fintech and Bajaj Finserv, and a half-year for Max Financial. Their figures should not be added or ranked against each other. The summaries do not include management commentary, guidance or the notes to the accounts, and none of the numbers has been checked against the original filings by this article.

How to verify

Readers who want to rely on the figures should consult the results filings that each company files with the BSE and NSE, which include the full financial statements and any reconciliations. Until then, the figures here are best treated as reported by the secondary source rather than confirmed.
source_name: Investywise summaries of company results (PB Fintech, October 30, 2026; Max Financial Services, October 27, 2026; Bajaj Finserv, board approval November 3, 2026)
image_alt: Stock market screens representing listed Indian financial companies' results (illustrative)
key_points: PB Fintech, the parent of Policybazaar and Paisabazaar, reported second-quarter FY27 profit after tax of Rs 192 crore, up 43%, on operating revenue of Rs 2,178 crore, up 35%, with total insurance premium of Rs 9,385 crore, up 38%.

Bajaj Finserv's consolidated profit after tax was Rs 5,952 crore against Rs 4,746 crore, up 25%, on total income of Rs 43,416 crore, up 17%; Bajaj Life Insurance's value of new business was Rs 512 crore, up 40%.

Max Financial Services reported first-half consolidated profit after tax of Rs 219 crore, up 137%, with Axis Max Life's annualised premium equivalent at Rs 4,638 crore, up 11%, and value of new business at Rs 1,180 crore, up 21%.
Axis Max Life's solvency ratio was 197%, and its claims paid ratio for FY26 was 99.8%, according to the summary.
All figures come from secondary summaries of company results, and the stock-exchange filings themselves were not reviewed for this article.
why_it_matters: India's life and general insurers, online distributors and lenders are closely watched because the country's insurance penetration is still developing and the government has opened the sector to full foreign ownership. These results show whether demand for protection products, online distribution and credit is translating into profit at three of the sector's best-known listed groups.
